opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think they tell us less than people often assume, though not nothing.

The classic examples are things like modified riddles. You take a well-known puzzle, like the surgeon riddle or a river-crossing problem, change one detail so the answer becomes trivial, and the model pattern-matches to the famous version and gives the canonical answer anyway. People point at that and say, "See, it's not really reasoning, it's just autocomplete." I get why that's compelling. It does reveal something real: these systems have strong priors from training, and sometimes those priors override careful reading of the actual question.

But I'd make a few points. First, humans fail at trick questions all the time. The bat-and-ball problem, the Cognitive Reflection Test, the Moses illusion, "how many animals of each kind did Moses take on the ark." Lots of very smart people get these wrong because they're running on fast heuristics. We don't conclude that those people can't reason. We conclude that heuristics sometimes misfire and that attention is limited. So a failure on an adversarially constructed question is weak evidence about general capability. It's mostly evidence about a specific failure mode.

Second, these failures have been declining quickly. A lot of the gotcha examples that went viral a couple of years ago are now handled fine, especially by models that think for a while before answering. When a model can reason step by step and check itself, it catches far more of these. So if your argument that AI is fundamentally limited rests on a particular trick question, you should expect it to have a short shelf life.

Third, and I think this matters most, what we care about for forecasting impact, including risk, is whether systems can do economically and strategically important work: write and debug substantial software, run research experiments, operate autonomously over long tasks. Performance on those things is measured much more directly by realistic task evaluations than by riddles. A system could keep falling for some cute trick and still be very capable at automating meaningful chunks of AI R&D. Conversely, acing every trick question wouldn't show it can do long-horizon agentic work.

That said, I don't want to fully dismiss them. Some trick-question failures point at real weaknesses: models can be overconfident, read sloppily, latch onto surface features, or fail to notice when something is off-distribution. Those weaknesses do matter for reliability in long tasks, where one misread instruction compounds. So I'd treat them as a useful probe of robustness and calibration, not as a test of whether there's "real intelligence" in there. The framing of "it fails this one riddle, therefore it doesn't understand anything" is the part I think is pretty misleading.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI failures as heuristic misfires and says they are weak evidence about general capability, not proof that the system cannot reason.

r002.rationale: It explains that a model may match an altered riddle to its familiar version and give the canonical answer because strong training priors override careful reading.

fable-5.1.text:
I think they tell us something, but people tend to overread them. When a model fails a trick question — like a slightly modified version of a classic riddle where the "obvious" answer is wrong — what you're mostly seeing is that the model has a strong prior from training data and isn't always checking whether the prior actually applies. That's a real limitation. It's a kind of pattern-matching failure, and it does show up in more practically relevant settings too, like when a model confidently applies a familiar approach to a problem that's subtly different.

But I'd push back on the inference that goes "it failed this trick question, therefore it can't really reason" or "therefore it's much less capable than it looks." Humans fail trick questions constantly. That's why they're called trick questions — they're specifically designed to exploit fast, heuristic responding. If you ask a smart person a bat-and-ball type question quickly, a lot of them get it wrong, and we don't conclude they can't do arithmetic.

The thing I actually care about is: how does the system do on tasks that matter, over longer horizons, when it's given a chance to think? And there, the trajectory has been pretty clear. Models have gotten dramatically better at things like agentic software engineering, hard math problems, and tasks that require sustained work, while there's still some set of trick questions you can construct that trips them up. Those two facts coexist. I think the trick-question failures are informative about the shape of the capability profile — it's jagged, it's not like a human profile — but they're not that informative about the overall level or the trajectory.

One more thing I'd say: a lot of the trick questions that used to work get fixed fairly quickly, sometimes just because they end up in the training data. So the specific failures aren't stable evidence. What is somewhat stable is the general pattern that models can be overconfident in a cached answer, and I think that's worth tracking — partly for capability reasons, but also for safety reasons, because a model that doesn't notice when a situation is subtly different from what it expects is a model you have to be more careful about trusting.

r001.rationale: The response describes failures as driven by strong priors and fast heuristics, and says they do not show that a model cannot reason.

r002.rationale: It gives a slightly modified classic riddle as an example and explains that training creates a strong prior the model may apply without checking whether it fits.

astra-6.text:
I think they tell you something, but you have to be pretty careful about what you’re inferring. If a model gets a trick question wrong, that’s evidence that it’s unreliable on that particular kind of question. It’s not necessarily strong evidence that it can’t do much harder things in other domains.

One distinction is between being able to solve a problem and reliably noticing when you need to think carefully. A model might give an intuitive, wrong answer, but then work out the right answer if you ask it to check its reasoning. That’s still a real failure—you might need the system to notice the problem without someone prompting it—but it suggests a different limitation from simply lacking the capability.

I’d want to know whether the failure persists across different phrasings, whether the model can explain its mistake, and whether it makes similar mistakes in realistic tasks. You shouldn’t dismiss these examples, but I also wouldn’t take a single striking failure as establishing some general ceiling on the system’s intelligence. The capabilities can be quite uneven.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes an unreliable or intuitive answer from lacking capability, but it does not say that trick-question failures may reflect cognitive biases.

r002.rationale: It does not describe a model applying a familiar riddle’s solution to an altered version or explain a training-created heuristic toward that answer.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they tell you something, but you have to be pretty careful about what you infer. A system can be very capable at solving difficult problems and still have a tendency to give the first answer that comes to mind when a question looks familiar. If you give it a slightly modified version of a classic puzzle, it might answer the classic puzzle instead of the question you actually asked.

That’s a real failure. But there are different explanations for it. Maybe the system can’t reason through the problem, or maybe it can reason through it but doesn’t reliably notice when it needs to. Those have different implications. One useful test is whether a fairly generic instruction like “check your assumptions” lets it recover, versus whether you have to explain the key insight.

I’d also distinguish intelligence from reliability. If you’re using the system to do something consequential, these mistakes matter even if it has the underlying capability. But I wouldn’t take a handful of surprising failures as evidence that all of its successes on harder tasks are somehow fake. You want to understand the pattern: when it fails, why it fails, and how much help it needs to get the right answer.

r001.rationale: The response says a capable system may give a familiar answer because it does not reliably notice when the question differs, rather than being unable to reason through it.

r002.rationale: It describes answering a classic puzzle when given a modified version, but does not attribute that tendency to training creating a strong heuristic.
